title: Compare ‘Big 4’ accounting firms vs. boutique R&D shops for tax credits
description: Choosing between a Big 4 firm and a boutique R&D tax credit advisor turns on fee basis, staffing and return coordination, not credit rates.
summary: Choosing between a Big 4 accounting firm and a boutique R&D tax credit advisor in the USA turns on fee basis, staffing, and tax-return coordination, not credit rates, which IRC § 41 sets. Big 4 auditors face PCAOB limits on contingent fees for audit clients, while boutiques avoid those rules but must coordinate § 174A positions with the return preparer.

body.text: Choosing between a Big 4 accounting firm and a boutique R&D tax credit advisor in the USA turns on fee basis, staffing, and tax-return coordination, not credit rates, which IRC § 41 sets. Big 4 auditors face PCAOB limits on contingent fees for audit clients, while boutiques avoid those rules but must coordinate § 174A positions with the return preparer.
Scope note. Broader federal R&D tax mechanics appear only where they change what a taxpayer should expect from either type of adviser.
1. What Both Types of Adviser Are Working With: The IRC § 41 Credit
1.1 Credit rates

The federal research credit is in Internal Revenue Code § 41 (26 U.S.C. § 41, as amended through Pub. L. 119-21 of July 4, 2025). That range comes from a practitioner's marketing page (Abdo Solutions describes 7-15% as a "typical benefit"), not from the statute. The statute itself sets these rates:

cells: Excess of qualified research expenses (QREs) over a base amount
QREs above 50% of the average QREs for the three prior years
ASC, no QREs in any one of the three prior years

body.text: Correction. The 7-15% figure is a provider's description of typical outcomes, not a rate set by law. The effective percentage depends on the method chosen, the taxpayer's base-period history, and, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, the Section 280C(c) adjustment described in Section 1.2 below.
1.2 Hypothetical worked example (ASC)
Hypothetical, for illustration only. The first part shows the gross ASC amount. The second part shows the effect of the Section 280C(c) adjustment that now applies to most taxpayers.

items: Current-year QREs: $1,000,000. Average QREs for the three prior years: $600,000.
50% of the prior-year average: $600,000 × 0.50 = $300,000.
ASC at 14%: $700,000 × 0.14 = $98,000, which is 9.8% of current-year QREs.
Same company with no QREs in one of the prior three years: $1,000,000 × 0.06 = $60,000 (6%).

body.text: Update: Section 280C(c) after July 2025. Pub. L. 119-21 amended § 280C(c)(1) so that, for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, a taxpayer's domestic research or experimental expenditures that are deducted or charged to capital account under new § 174A must be reduced by the amount of the § 41 credit allowed, unless the taxpayer elects a reduced credit under § 280C(c)(2). Practitioner commentary describes the practical effect as roughly a 21% reduction in the net credit benefit for most corporate taxpayers (the 21% corporate rate applied to the credit amount). On the example above, a $98,000 gross ASC would yield roughly $77,420 of net benefit to a C corporation at the 21% rate under either route. This arithmetic is identical whoever prepares the claim, but it does change the size of the benefit against which any percentage-of-benefit fee (Section 3.3) is measured, and an adviser should explain the election choice rather than quoting the gross figure.

Analysis. Whoever prepares the claim, Big 4 or boutique, the statutory arithmetic is the same. The two models really differ on how many qualifying activities and costs they find, how well they document them, and how carefully they handle the elections that now interact with § 174A, not on the rate.
1.3 Payroll tax election for start-ups

Section 41(h) supports this. A "qualified small business" must have gross receipts under $5,000,000 for the year and no gross receipts for any year before the five-year period ending with the current year. The election is capped at $250,000. For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022, § 41(h)(4)(B)(i)(II) raises that cap by a further $250,000. That increase was added by Pub. L. 117-169 (the Inflation Reduction Act) on August 16, 2022, which means up to $500,000 in total. The additional $250,000 can be applied only against the employer share of Medicare hospital insurance tax, not against the employer share of Social Security tax, so the full $500,000 is usable only by a company with enough Medicare-tax liability. The payroll offset is claimed on Form 6765 and then on Form 8974 with the employer's quarterly payroll return (Form 941).

Analysis. This election is the main route by which a pre-revenue start-up gets cash value from the credit, so it is the subtopic on which boutique providers most often market to Series A-B companies (Section 3.2). Qualified small businesses that make the payroll election are also exempt from the new Section G reporting on Form 6765 (Section 5), which lowers the documentation burden for that segment regardless of provider type.
1.4 The four-part test
Under § 41(d)(1), qualified research must be:

items: research with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under § 174A;
undertaken to discover information that is technological in nature;
intended to be useful in developing a new or improved business component; and
research in which substantially all of the activities are elements of a process of experimentation.

body.text: Correction / update. Pub. L. 119-21 (July 4, 2025, commonly called the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act") amended § 41(d)(1)(A). The earlier text referred to expenditures that "may be treated as specified research or experimental expenditures under section 174." The amended text reads "with respect to which expenditures are treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under section 174A." New § 174A allows domestic research or experimental expenditures to be deducted currently for amounts paid or incurred in tax years beginning after December 31, 2024; foreign research expenditures remain under § 174 and continue to be amortized over 15 years. IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-28 provides the procedures for adopting the new rules.

Why the wording change matters for the comparison. Several law firms have noted that "are treated" appears to be a stricter test than the old "may be treated." On an original return, a taxpayer can satisfy it by deducting or otherwise accounting for its QREs under § 174A. On an amended-return refund claim, it may be harder: if additional costs being claimed as QREs were not originally accounted for as § 174A expenditures, treating them that way can require a change in accounting method, which generally cannot be made on an amended return. Rev. Proc. 2025-28 gave certain taxpayers, including small businesses with average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less, a limited window to file amended returns and make related elections; that window closed on July 6, 2026.

Analysis. This makes coordination between the R&D credit study and the taxpayer's § 174A accounting more important than it was before. A Big 4 firm that also prepares the client's federal return can coordinate the two directly. A boutique that prepares only the credit study must coordinate with whoever prepares the return. Neither model is inherently better here, but a taxpayer should ask any candidate provider how it ensures that every QRE claimed is also treated under § 174A.
Section 41(d)(3)(B) adds that research is not treated as conducted for a permitted purpose if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors.
2. The Big 4 Model: Claims Checked
2.1 Conflict of interest between audit and advisory work

Revenue mix. Published fiscal-year 2024 figures do not support this. Statista's compilation of 2024 revenue by function, which is a secondary source, gives the figures below; PwC's own 2024 Transparency Report confirms its assurance revenue of $19.475 billion out of $55.4 billion in gross revenue, and notes that audit accounts for about three-quarters of PwC's assurance revenue.

Notes on the table: Statista labels Deloitte's assurance line "Audit and enterprise risk services," which is broader than statutory audit. Deloitte's and EY's figures also include an "other" category (Deloitte financial advisory of about $5 billion; EY transaction advisory of about $6.2 billion) that is not shown in a separate column. Fiscal years differ: Deloitte's ends May 31, PwC's and EY's end June 30, and KPMG's ends September 30.

Update: fiscal-year 2025 totals. All four firms have since reported fiscal-year 2025 results: Deloitte $70.5 billion, PwC $56.9 billion, EY $53.2 billion, and KPMG $39.8 billion. PwC's assurance revenue rose to $19.8 billion, about 34.8% of its total, against $24.3 billion in advisory and $12.7 billion in tax and legal services. The full functional split for the other three firms was not available in the sources checked, but the reported growth rates by service line (for example, Deloitte's Audit & Assurance grew 3.8% in local currency, slightly slower than its other businesses) do not suggest any material change from the 2024 pattern.

On these figures, audit is roughly one-third of revenue at each of the four firms, not one-fifth. Non-audit work (consulting, advisory, tax and other) is about two-thirds, which is a majority but not a "vast" one. Tax alone is roughly 17% to 23% of each firm's revenue.
Regulatory response.

items: UK. On July 6, 2020, the Financial Reporting Council (FRC) published principles for operational separation (ring-fencing) of the Big Four's audit practices. Full implementation was due by June 30, 2024 at the latest. The FRC revised the principles in February 2021. This requires ring-fencing inside each firm, not a spin-off.

USA. No U.S. separation mandate was found. U.S. rules instead limit what tax services an auditor may provide to an audit client. PCAOB Rule 3521 treats a registered firm as not independent if it provides any service or product to an audit client for a contingent fee or commission. Rule 3522 bars services that market, plan or opine in favor of confidential transactions or aggressive tax position transactions. Rule 3523 bars tax services to persons in a financial reporting oversight role at the audit client. Rule 3524 requires the auditor, before tax services are pre-approved, to describe in writing to the audit committee the scope of the service and the fee structure, discuss the potential effects on independence, and document that discussion. The SEC approved Rules 3521 through 3524 in April 2006.

body.text: Analysis. The U.S. independence rules bear directly on this comparison. When the Big 4 firm is also the client's auditor and the client is subject to PCAOB rules (an issuer or other audit client of a registered firm), the firm cannot take the R&D study on a contingent (percentage-of-credit) fee, and the engagement needs audit-committee pre-approval after the Rule 3524 disclosures. This cuts both ways. For a private company that is not subject to PCAOB rules, AICPA independence rules apply instead; those rules were not reviewed for this report.
Wirecard and Carillion.

items: Wirecard (EY, Germany). Germany's auditor oversight body APAS ruled on March 30-31, 2023 that professional duties were breached in the audits of Wirecard AG and Wirecard Bank AG for 2016-2018. It fined the audit firm €500,000 and barred it from accepting new public-interest-entity audit mandates for two years (Bloomberg Law, April 3, 2023; Bloomberg Tax, May 11, 2023). APAS did not name EY, but Wirecard's annual reports list EY as auditor.

Carillion (KPMG, UK). On October 12, 2023, the FRC fined KPMG LLP £18.55 million and KPMG Audit Plc £2.45 million (£21 million in total, after a 30% discount for cooperation) over the Carillion audits (AccountingWEB; Bloomberg Tax). The FRC also criticized the close relationship between KPMG and Carillion as a risk to objectivity.

body.text: Clarification. Both cases were audit-quality enforcement actions outside the United States. Neither found that conflicts arising from consulting or tax work caused the failures. They show regulatory concern about objectivity in general. They are not evidence about the quality of U.S. R&D tax credit claims prepared by either type of provider.
2.2 Personnel continuity and seniority

items: Turnover. Erin L. MacLean's 2013 Claremont McKenna thesis examines high turnover across Deloitte, EY, KPMG and PwC. It describes turnover as costly in training and in lost knowledge and experience. The thesis is from 2013 and is not specific to R&D tax. More recent headcount data show the issue persists in a different form: PwC, for example, reported a global headcount of about 364,000 in fiscal 2025, down from more than 370,000 the year before, and dropped a previously announced hiring target. Headcount reduction is not the same as turnover, but it signals that staffing on any given engagement can change from year to year.

Junior staffing. Apex Advisors (2017) says especially large firms may put their larger clients first, so a smaller client's study may be done by less-qualified seniors and staff. The same article also says boutiques may lack the staff to maximize a credit. Nothing reviewed supports the claim that clients must re-educate new staff every year.

Client time burden. The "200+ hours annually" figure comes from a Thomson Reuters / Neo.Tax product blog (September 8, 2025). It says tax and R&D teams spend over 200 hours a year coordinating interviews. That blog is vendor marketing and refers to "traditional accounting firms" generally, not to the Big 4.

body.text: 2.3 Fees and methodology

items: "$100,000 to $500,000" fees. This appears in the same Thomson Reuters / Neo.Tax marketing blog, which says traditional accounting firms charge $100,000 to $500,000. It is a vendor's characterization, not survey data, and it is not specific to the Big 4.

Estimates and after-the-fact documentation. The same blog says interview-based estimates and after-the-fact documentation fall short of IRS standards. That concern is consistent with the IRS's own refund-claim requirements and the new Section G of Form 6765 (Section 5), both of which push toward contemporaneous, business-component-level documentation.

body.text: 3. The Boutique Model: Claims Checked
3.1 "Pure play" focus

Analysis. A pure-play provider that does not audit the client is outside the PCAOB auditor-independence rules described in Section 2.1, so it may use contingent fees where a Big 4 auditor could not. That is a structural difference, not a quality difference. It also means the main external check on fee-driven aggressiveness for that provider is the IRS's own penalty and preparer regime rather than auditor-independence rules.
3.2 Claimed outcome figures

items: "Series A-B companies miss $100K-$500K annually" and "general accountants miss 80%." Both figures appear in an Asnani CPA blog post (November 4, 2025). The page cites no source for either figure.

$847,000 missed savings. The Asnani post attributes this to one AI start-up founder over three years. Correction: the total covers R&D credits plus the Employee Retention Credit, California's New Employment Credit and other incentives. It is not an R&D-only figure, so it does not show what an R&D specialist alone recovered.

$840,000 case study. Smith and Howard reports securing about $840,000 in combined federal and Georgia credits for a SaaS client through an interview cycle and data analysis. Correction: Smith and Howard is a multi-service CPA firm that offers assurance among other services.

body.text: 3.3 Multidisciplinary teams and fee structures

items: Team composition. Source Advisors says its in-house team includes project managers, CPAs, attorneys and engineers.

Fixed fees and included audit support. Source Advisors says it charges a fixed fee based on project scope rather than a percentage of the benefit, and that the fee includes audit support through appeals at no extra cost.

Percentage-of-benefit fees. That article is about the UK regime administered by HMRC, not the U.S. federal credit. It also gives two different boutique ranges: 15-30% in the text and 10-30% in its table. For accountancy practices it gives 5-15%. No comparable U.S. survey of contingent-fee ranges was found.

body.text: Hypothetical fee illustration. Hypothetical; it uses the UK-sourced ranges only to show the arithmetic. On the $98,000 gross credit from Section 1.2, a 10-30% fee would be $9,800-$29,400, and a 15-30% fee would be $14,700-$29,400. If the fee is instead measured against the roughly $77,420 net benefit after the Section 280C(c) adjustment, the same percentages produce $7,742-$23,226 and $11,613-$23,226. A taxpayer should confirm in the engagement letter whether a percentage fee is computed on the gross or the net credit. A Big 4 firm that is also the client's auditor could not use this contingent model where PCAOB Rule 3521 applies.

cells: Audit, tax and advisory. Audit was about 31-35% of fiscal 2024 revenue at all four firms
For PCAOB audit clients: no contingent fees, no confidential or aggressive tax position transaction services, audit-committee pre-approval required
Not subject to auditor-independence rules if it does not audit the client
Can coordinate directly if it also prepares the return
Must coordinate with the client's return preparer
High turnover documented across the Big 4 (2013 study). Smaller clients may get less-senior staff
Engineers, CPAs and attorneys on staff (provider claims). May lack scale (Apex)
"$100K-$500K" attributed to traditional firms by a vendor blog
"200+ hours" attributed to traditional methods by a vendor blog
Unverified as a Big 4 vs. boutique comparison

body.text: 5. Audit Risk and Sustaining the Claim

items: Audit likelihood. Aprio says claiming the credit does not by itself trigger an audit. It also says an unsuccessful audit can mean full disallowance and possible penalties, and recommends gathering qualitative documentation early.

IRS documentation focus. For research credit refund claims postmarked on or after January 10, 2022, the IRS requires five items of information: the business components to which the claim relates; for each business component, the research activities performed; the individuals who performed each activity; the information each individual sought to discover; and the total qualified employee wage, supply and contract research expenses for the claim year. Form 6765 may be used for the expense totals. In June 2024 the IRS modified these requirements, so that refund claims postmarked after June 18, 2024 must identify all business components and their related research activities and provide the expense totals, while the names of individuals and the information each sought are no longer required at the time of filing. The five items apply to formal and informal claims, and Form 1120 filers must use a formal amended return. During a transition period, a deficient claim is notified by letter and the taxpayer has 45 days to perfect it before the IRS makes a final determination. Update: the IRS has extended that transition period several times; on October 1, 2025 (IR-2025-99) it extended it through January 10, 2027.

New Section G of Form 6765. The IRS revised Form 6765 to add Section G, which requires QREs and research information to be reported at the business-component level on the original return. Section G was optional for tax year 2024, and the IRS announced on October 1, 2025 that it would remain optional for all filers for tax year 2025, with mandatory reporting expected from tax year 2026 onward. Exemptions include qualified small businesses that elect the payroll tax offset, and taxpayers with total QREs of $1.5 million or less and gross receipts of $50 million or less. For a provider of either type, Section G means that business-component-level documentation must exist when the original return is filed, not only when an examination starts.
Bundled audit defense. Source Advisors includes audit support through appeals in its fixed fee. That some providers treat audit defense as a separate paid engagement was not verified.

body.text: Analysis. The refund-claim requirements apply to amended-return claims, and Section G will apply to most original-return claims, whoever prepares them. The best evidence of a provider's value is whether its work product meets these requirements and holds up on examination.
6. Conclusions

items: Supported. Regulators treat audit-plus-tax work as an independence risk. The FRC requires ring-fenced audit practices in the UK, and PCAOB rules restrict fee structures and certain tax services for audit clients. A boutique that does not audit the client is outside those constraints.

Qualified. Audit is about a third of Big 4 revenue at all four firms, not a fifth. The Wirecard and Carillion cases were non-U.S. audit-quality failures, not findings about tax-credit conflicts. Post-2025 changes to §§ 41(d)(1)(A), 174A and 280C(c) make coordination with the client's tax return more important, which can favor a provider that also prepares the return.

Weak evidence. The headline figures on time burden, fees and missed savings come from vendor or marketing content. Two case figures belong to a general CPA firm or include non-R&D credits, and one fee range is from the UK.

body.text: A business choosing between the two models can test the claims that matter by asking any candidate firm five things: whether it is the company's auditor and how that affects its fee basis; who will actually staff the study; how it will meet the IRS refund-claim requirements and the new Section G business-component reporting; how it will make sure every QRE claimed is also treated under § 174A and how it will advise on the § 280C(c) election; and what audit support the fee includes.
